meta.title: A spin on Hagedorn temperatures and string stars
meta.abstractHtml: We discuss the correspondence between highly excited strings and black holes in the presence of angular momentum. At fixed imaginary angular velocity , we show that free strings exhibit a Hagedorn instability due to a thermal-winding mode turning tachyonic. This allows us to determine the exact Hagedorn temperature for bosonic, type II, and heterotic strings. Using the effective field theory for the thermal-winding mode around the -dependent background, we find a novel ‘rotating string star’ saddle (perturbatively in the angular velocity) and study its properties. This configuration describes a self-gravitating bound state of highly excited rotating strings. As in the non-rotating case, the saddle is qualitatively shown to interpolate between the rotating strings phase and a rotating black hole. We also comment on the implications of these results for anti-de Sitter space.

children.title: Abstract
children.body: We discuss the correspondence between highly excited strings and black holes in the presence of angular momentum. At fixed imaginary angular velocity , we show that free strings exhibit a Hagedorn instability due to a thermal-winding mode turning tachyonic. This allows us to determine the exact Hagedorn temperature for bosonic, type II, and heterotic strings. Using the effective field theory for the thermal-winding mode around the -dependent background, we find a novel ‘rotating string star’ saddle (perturbatively in the angular velocity) and study its properties. This configuration describes a self-gravitating bound state of highly excited rotating strings. As in the non-rotating case, the saddle is qualitatively shown to interpolate between the rotating strings phase and a rotating black hole. We also comment on the implications of these results for anti-de Sitter space.

Over time, black holes tend to shrink as they radiate. The fate of small (highly-curved) black holes in a UV-complete theory of gravity is therefore an interesting self-consistency check [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], which could teach us a lesson on black hole microscopy. In string theory, the nature of black holes as their horizon size reaches the string scale remains an open question [8, 9, 10, 11]. One version of this question is phrased in terms of Euclidean gravity [12]. The Euclidean black hole saddle in asymptotically string theory1 is well described by Einstein gravity for , but what is its description for ? Horowitz and Polchinski [15] suggested that at high temperatures and for , the saddle is a normalizable condensate of strings winding on the thermal cycle of . The saddle, interpreted as a self-gravitating stringy condensate [16, 17], is termed ‘the Horowitz-Polchinski solution’ or a ‘string star’. Surprisingly, this saddle carries an thermal entropy, and qualitatively agrees with black hole thermodynamics at lower temperatures.2 Recently, there has been a renewed interest in string stars, extending the original setting [12, 18] to higher dimensions  [19, 20, 21, 22, 23], and other background geometries [14, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30].

gist.html: Poses the question: what does a Euclidean black hole become at string size? Horowitz and Polchinski proposed a string star.

children.title: The black hole/string correspondence
children.body: A black hole of mass $M$ in $D$ dimensions has a horizon that shrinks as it radiates, and its temperature rises. When the horizon reaches the string length $l_s$, curvature is of string size and general relativity stops being reliable. Susskind, and Horowitz and Polchinski, noticed that at this point the black hole's entropy is comparable to that of a single highly excited string of the same mass, which grows linearly with $M$. This correspondence principle suggests that the black hole does not end abruptly but turns into strings, perhaps a ball of string bound by its own gravity. In the Euclidean language used here, the black hole and that self-gravitating string are two saddles of the same thermal partition function, and the claim is that one deforms into the other as the temperature changes. The paper asks whether the same picture survives when the black hole rotates.

To gather more evidence for this proposal, it is natural to consider extra parameters to turn on, both at the string star and the black hole sides of the correspondence. In this work, we study the correspondence in the presence of angular momenta.3 Let be a rotation generator in a two-dimensional plane of . To add angular momenta, we consider an ensemble of fixed temperature , and fixed imaginary ‘angular velocity’ potential , conjugate to , with the partition function

(1.1)

In terms of Euclidean string theory, this ensemble is defined by an asymptotic boundary condition with a twist between the thermal and the angular directions. The twisted is one possible saddle that contributes to , describing, at , freely rotating strings. The Euclidean rotating black hole is another saddle with the same asymptotics that contributes to (1.1). This work suggests a description of the rotating black hole saddle when it reaches a string size . Following the non-rotating case, we find a normalizable winding condensate solution on top of the twisted background. The result is a ‘rotating string star’ saddle, interpreted as a bound state of self-gravitating rotating strings. By studying the saddle thermodynamic properties, we find a qualitative agreement with the rotating black hole (see figure 1).

gist.html: Adds angular momentum at fixed imaginary angular velocity $\nu$; a rotating string star qualitatively matches the rotating black hole.

We give two alternative ways to find (1.2). One is to directly check the Hagedorn growth of the partition function due to high-energy excitations. A second, more instructive way for our purposes is to follow [42, 43, 13] and interpret the Hagedorn instability as a tachyonic instability of a thermal winding mode in . Studying the winding sector of the twisted worldsheet theory, we were able to derive (1.2). As we explain, it is also possible to derive (1.2) perturbatively in from a target space analysis. Using a Kaluza-Klein (KK) reduction, we find a novel ( dependent) effective field theory (EFT) for the thermal winding mode on . In this way, the Hagedorn temperature (1.2) is the temperature at which a winding mode turns massless.

children.body: In section 3, we follow [15] and employ this -dimensional EFT of the winding mode coupled to gravity to find a normalizable winding condensate, or a rotating string star.6 To find the solution, we employ perturbation theory in , which to leading order amounts to a rigid-body approximation. By analytically continuing the solution back to real angular velocity (), we write down the thermodynamic properties of the rotating string star saddle. The rotating string star shares many properties with the non-rotating solution, such as entropy. The winding profile is invariant to the remaining rotation symmetry group and thus has no intrinsic spin. Notably, this solution still carries a non-zero angular momentum, due to the non-trivial dependence, similar to the rotating black hole. In section 4, we compare these properties to rotating black holes and to free strings. As in the non-rotating case, we find qualitative agreement between both in their intermediate parameter regimes.

gist.html: Perturbatively in $\nu$, the winding theory with gravity gives a rotating string star: no intrinsic spin, yet $O(G_N^{-1})$ angular momentum.

children.body: Finally, in section 5 we follow [14, 24] and discuss the extension of our results to anti-de Sitter (AdS) space. We compute the leading behavior of the AdS Hagedorn temperature in , and comment on the expected properties of the rotating AdS string star.

gist.html: In AdS, the leading $l_s/l_{ads}$ shift of the Hagedorn temperature is computed and the rotating AdS string star discussed.
With imaginary rotation, free strings keep a Hagedorn instability, and a rotating string star bridges rotating strings and black holes.

brief.html: A string-size Euclidean black hole has been proposed to become a string star, a self-gravitating condensate of wound strings; the paper tests this with rotation. The paper adds angular momentum through an imaginary angular velocity $\nu$, a twist of the thermal circle. Free strings then keep a Hagedorn instability, at an exact $\nu$-dependent temperature where a winding mode turns massless. That mode, coupled to gravity, forms a rotating string star that qualitatively matches rotating black holes and rotating strings. AdS is treated last.

children.title: Why string states grow exponentially
children.body: A free closed string's mass is set by its oscillator level $N$, with $\alpha'M^2\approx4N$ per side. The number of states at level $N$ is the number of ways to share $N$ among the oscillators of all transverse directions, a partition problem. Its asymptotics follow from the Cardy formula: the count grows like $e^{2\pi\sqrt{cN/6}}$, with $c$ the number of transverse worldsheet fields. Since $\sqrt N$ is proportional to $M$, the number of string states grows exponentially in the mass, $e^{\beta_HM}$, and the entropy linearly. A gas of strings at temperature $T$ weighs each state by $e^{-M/T}$; above $T_H=1/\beta_H$ the growth wins and the partition function diverges. This is the Hagedorn temperature, $1/(4\pi\sqrt{\alpha'})$ for bosonic strings. The paper finds the same exponential growth when the states are also weighted by the phase of their angular momentum, with a rate that depends on that phase.

children.title: Imaginary angular velocity as a twisted circle
children.body: The grand canonical trace $\operatorname{Tr}\,e^{- eta(H-\Omega J)}$ becomes, as a Euclidean path integral, an integral over fields on space times a circle of length $ eta$. The factor $e^{ eta\Omega J}$ is a rotation; for imaginary $\Omega$, with $ eta\Omega=2\pi i u$, it rotates the plane of $J$ by the real angle $2\pi u$. The trace then glues the end of Euclidean time to its start after this rotation: fields obey $\Phi( au+ eta)=e^{-2\pi i u}\Phi( au)$ for the complex coordinate of that plane. Space stays locally flat; only the identification is twisted. Since $e^{2\pi iJ}$ is $1$ for integer spins and $(-1)^F$ for half-integer ones, $ u$ is periodic with period 1 for bosonic theories and 2 for theories with fermions, where $ u=1$ inserts $(-1)^F$. A rotating Euclidean black hole is a real metric for such imaginary angular velocity. The paper's thermal strings, black holes and string stars all live with this twisted boundary condition.

The first thing to note about this ensemble is that the imaginary angular velocity is actually compact. Since for the bosonic theory states have integer , the partition function is periodic in , namely . Due to half-integer , for superstring theories we expect . Secondly, an imaginary angular velocity also means that the canonical ensemble is no longer dominated by maximally rotating strings. This is because instead of exponential growth, the Boltzmann factor only acquires a phase . This opens the possibility that at fixed the high energy behavior will be dominated by Hagedorn growth of the entropy, accompanied by the phases coming from the angular momentum term. The main result of this section is that this ensemble indeed possesses a non-trivial Hagedorn instability. More precisely, we claim that the partition function diverges above some temperature , for some function .

brief.html: Fixing a real angular velocity in flat space gives a divergent ensemble, because arbitrarily large angular momentum costs little energy. An imaginary angular velocity, $ eta\Omega=2\pi i u$, turns the rotation weight into a phase, makes $ u$ periodic, and is the ensemble where rotating black holes are real. Counting bosonic string states, the partition function still diverges above a Hagedorn temperature, now with $R_H^2/\alpha'=4+2 u( u-1)$: the phases at first raise the temperature, which returns at $ u=1$.

children.body: Following the work of [42, 43, 13], there is a second, intuitive way to explain the Hagedorn instability of string theory in the canonical ensemble. The idea is to follow [57], and understand the canonical partition function as the Euclidean string theory partition function on (with anti-periodic boundary condition for the fermions). In terms of the Euclidean theory, the Hagedorn instability is a divergence of the 1-loop path integral in this background. Unlike field theory, string theory in this background includes sectors of strings winding around the thermal circle. Due to their extension along the thermal circle, the mass of the winding strings is, up to an overall constant, proportional to . A direct computation shows that the lightest winding mode turns massless at the Hagedorn temperature , and tachyonic for higher temperatures. As it becomes massless, the 1-loop partition function acquires a new divergence at , and turns ill-defined for . This is the Euclidean reasoning behind the linear Hagedorn growth of the entropy.

gist.html: Recalls the Euclidean picture: the Hagedorn divergence is a wound string on the thermal circle turning massless, then tachyonic.

children.title: Twisted sectors and shifted zero-point energy
children.body: When a theory is quotiented by a symmetry, an orbifold, closed strings need only close up to that symmetry: these extra states form twisted sectors. Here a string wound once around the thermal circle must return with its rotation-plane coordinate rotated by $e^{2\pi i u}$, so its oscillator frequencies shift from integers $n$ to $|n+ u|$. The mass of a string state includes the zero-point energy of all its oscillators, a divergent sum regulated by the Riemann zeta function: $\sum_{n\ge1}n=- rac1{12}$, and the shifted sum $\sum_n(n+ u)$ gives a $ u$-dependent answer. A single twisted complex boson therefore changes the ground-state energy of the wound string by a quadratic polynomial in $ u$. children.title: The GSO projection and the lightest level
children.body: The Ramond–Neveu–Schwarz superstring has worldsheet fermions, and its spectrum contains a tachyon at the lowest level. The Gliozzi–Scherk–Olive (GSO) projection keeps only states of a definite worldsheet fermion number; it removes that tachyon and makes the theory supersymmetric and consistent. On a thermal circle the target-space fermions are antiperiodic, and wound strings then obey a different projection: the lowest level $N=0$ survives, and it is this state that turns tachyonic at the Hagedorn temperature. With periodic fermions, the supersymmetric case, the usual projection applies and the lowest allowed level is $N=1/2$. Inserting the rotation $e^{2\pi i u J}$ interpolates between the two, since $ u=1$ makes the fermions periodic. The paper therefore has to follow which level is allowed as $ u$ varies, and finds it changes at $| u|=1/2$.

The answer is that the GSO projection and the transformation are not commutative. Notice that at the creation and annihilation operators switch roles. children.body: In Kaluza–Klein reduction, a metric on space times a circle is written as $G_{tt}(dt-A_idx^i)^2$ plus a spatial metric: the off-diagonal components become a gauge field $A$, the circle's size a scalar, and momentum around the circle is the charge. Melvin space is flat space in which going around the circle rotates a plane by an angle $2\pi\nu$. In coordinates where the identification is untwisted, the metric acquires a cross term between the circle and the angle of the plane, so $A_\phi$ is non-zero: a magnetic field, concentrated near the rotation axis and falling off far from it, together with a varying circle size $G_{tt}=R^2+\nu^2\rho^2$. This is a magnetic flux tube, or fluxbrane. A string wound on the circle feels it through $G_{tt}$, which grows away from the axis and confines it near $\rho=0$, the mass term the paper finds.

One such saddle is the twisted itself, representing weakly-interacting thermal strings in flat space. Another is the (rotating) Euclidean black hole saddle, in which the thermal circle shrinks with an topology. This saddle remains under control (weakly-curved) only for . At and for temperatures close to the Hagdorn temperature, [15] found another type of saddle, a ‘string star’. Using the EFT found in [13] coupled to gravity, the authors found a normalizable condensate of the winding mode for - a string star. children.title: The Horowitz–Polchinski string star
children.body: Just below the Hagedorn temperature the thermal winding mode $\chi$ is light, with $m^2\propto R-R_H$, and can be described by a field theory in $d$ dimensions together with gravity, as Horowitz and Polchinski did. Its mass depends on the size of the thermal circle, which the Newtonian potential $\varphi$ changes: where the potential is negative the circle shrinks and the winding mode gets lighter. A condensate of $\chi$ sources $\varphi$, and $\varphi$ in turn lowers the mass of $\chi$, so the condensate can bind itself. The equations, $ abla^2\chi=m^2\chi+\kappa\varphi\chi$ and $ abla^2\varphi\propto|\chi|^2$, are scale invariant: the solution has size $1/m$ and amplitude of order $m^2$. Normalizable solutions exist for $3\le d\le5$ spatial dimensions; for $d\ge6$ they collapse. Their entropy obeys $S\approx eta_HM$, like free strings. This Horowitz–Polchinski solution is the original string star, and the paper perturbs it in the twist $ u$.

Analogously to the case, we work at temperatures close to the Hagedorn temperature . As the winding mode becomes parametrically light compared to the other stringy modes, we can look for saddles of the EFT derived in the previous section, together with gravity. Analogously to the nonrotating case [12, 15], we will keep only quadratic fluctuations of the metric and a cubic interaction of the metric components with the winding mode, and verify a posteriori that the solution is self-consistent. Due to the more complicated structure of the metric, more metric components couple at this order to the winding mode compared to the case, including also the dilaton.

gist.html: Near $R_H(\nu)$ the winding mode is light; quadratic gravity and cubic couplings suffice, with more metric components and the dilaton.

children.body: The main importance of the string star saddle was the suggestion by Horowitz and Polchinski [15] that it interpolates between the black hole and the free string phases of string theory. More precisely [12], the suggestion is that as a Euclidean saddle defined close to , it is continuously connected to the Euclidean black hole at lower temperatures . In other words, as the Euclidean black hole size reaches the string scale, its Einstein gravity description is no longer valid, and should now be described as a self-gravitating string. In this context, this is what is usually referred to as the correspondence principle, or the black hole-string transition. The main argument in favor of this suggestion was that extrapolating the thermodynamic properties of both saddles to an intermediate regime (where both are ill defined), gives qualitatively the same result.

gist.html: Recalls the correspondence principle: the string star would continue the Euclidean black hole to string-scale temperatures.

children.body: In the other direction, close enough to the Hagedorn temperature, the string star amplitude goes to zero, and we expect it to reduce to the free string phase of the thermal background. This is better described in terms of the microcanonical ensemble. The free string phase is expected to dominate the ensemble at low energies. For high enough energies, the free string self-gravitation can no longer be ignored, and we expect a transition to the string star description. Here as well, a simple extrapolation qualitatively gives the same answer.

gist.html: At the other end the star should reduce to free strings, best seen at fixed energy.

children.body: In four dimensions the rotating vacuum black hole is Kerr's. Myers and Perry found its generalisation to $D$ spacetime dimensions, where a black hole can rotate independently in each of $\lfloor(D-1)/2\rfloor$ planes. With rotation in a single plane, the solution has a mass parameter $\mu$ and a rotation parameter $a$, and its horizon radius $r_h$ solves $r_h^2+a^2=\mu/r_h^{D-5}$. Its mass, entropy and angular momentum follow, with $J\propto Ma$, as do its temperature and horizon angular velocity $\Omega=a/(r_h^2+a^2)$. For small $\Omega$ everything can be expanded about Schwarzschild, and the horizon flattens, with eccentricity proportional to $\Omega$. In $D\ge6$ such black holes can spin without bound and become very flat, the ultraspinning regime. The paper uses only the slow, single-plane case, extrapolated to string-scale temperature, to compare with its rotating string star.

Similarly, the (small) AdS black hole at high temperatures is well approximated by the Schwarzschild solution. As a result, the qualitative arguments for the string/black hole correspondence at intermediate temperatures in flat space immediately apply to AdS.

children.body: A nuanced version of this discussion exists for AdS. While in flat space no string star solutions exist, it was shown in [24] that such solutions do exist in AdS. Following [80], it was suggested that the AdS string star is continuously related to the ‘S-transformed’ BTZ solution deformed by an angular winding condensate (defined only for very low temperatures). Adding non-zero angular velocity, we expect a generalization of this discussion. In terms of the modular parameter , we can define the Hagedorn line . A reliable string star solution exists in a small region close to .27 Using the S-transformation , there also is a second region close to where we can find a reliable winding condensate, this time around the (rotating) BTZ solution. The string/BTZ transition suggested in  [80, 24] can be understood as the claim that these two regions are smoothly related as a function of .

gist.html: In AdS$_3$, rotation should extend the proposed string star/BTZ link between the Hagedorn line and its S-image.

children.body: We can also consider a more general transformation than just S. Of the entire modular group , only transformations that keep the boundary condition of the fermions map a string star solution to another one.28 The subgroup that fixes the boundary conditions is generated by and , and goes by the name the theta group  [81]. For its fundamental domain, we can take with . In this domain, the reliable winding condensate is an angular condensate of a very cold () rotating BTZ solution. A natural generalization of the string/BTZ transition suggestion would be that it is possible to extend the winding condensate solution in such a way that maps the solutions at the boundaries of the fundamental region to each other. If true, it means that all the mappings of the string star solution are continuously related to each other, in the same way the AdS string star is related to the BTZ solution.

gist.html: The theta group maps string stars to string stars, suggesting all its images are continuously related.
Small rotating AdS string stars should follow flat-space ones; in AdS$_3$, modular images hint at links to rotating BTZ.

brief.html: Somewhat below the AdS Hagedorn temperature, AdS string stars are small and look like flat-space ones, as do small AdS black holes, so the correspondence carries over. With rotation the paper estimates the star rather than solving it: rigid-body rotation with $\mathcal I\propto R-R_H$ near the AdS Hagedorn temperature, where real $\Omega$ is allowed directly. In AdS$_3$, the paper suggests that the images of the string star under the theta group, including winding condensates on cold rotating BTZ, may all be continuously related.

gist.html: In AdS the winding mode is stable at real angular velocity; the Hagedorn shift is computed, the rotating star estimated.

brief.html: In AdS the rotating ensemble is well defined even at finite coupling, with rotating thermal AdS and the rotating black hole as saddles. Curvature keeps the winding mode stable at real angular velocity below the unitarity bound, and fixes the leading $l_s/l_{ads}$ shift of $R_H$. In pure NS-NS AdS$_3$, type II's exact $R_H(\nu)$ equals flat space's for $k|\nu|>1$. Small AdS string stars look flat, so the rotating correspondence should carry over; near the AdS Hagedorn temperature real-$\Omega$ stars can be sought directly.

children.body: There are several natural generalizations of our work. One is to include more than one angular momentum (for ), and compare with the appropriate (Myers–Perry) black hole. Specifically for , one can turn on equal angular momenta for the and the directions, in which the string star equations are one-dimensional again (as in ). It would also be interesting to better understand the AdS rotating solutions, especially for pure NS-NS, where one could hope for an exact worldsheet description following [26]. In AdS, it is also common to turn on chemical potentials for rotations of internal direction [82] (dual on the CFT to global symmetries). gist.html:
• Context Does a string-size black hole become a self-gravitating “string star” when it rotates?
  • Result
    • At imaginary angular velocity $\nu$, a thermal winding mode turns tachyonic, giving exact Hagedorn temperatures $\beta_H(\nu)$ for bosonic, type II and heterotic strings.
    • A “rotating string star” saddle, found numerically to order $\nu^2$ for $3\le d\le5$, rotates rigidly with $O(1/G_N)$ angular momentum.
    • Extrapolated, its angular momentum and eccentricity match rotating black holes' and free strings' up to $O(1)$ factors: a qualitative interpolation.
    • In AdS, the Hagedorn temperature's leading $l_s/l_{ads}$ shift is computed at real or imaginary rotation.
  • Why it matters The rotating star is offered as what a rotating black hole becomes at string size.

specialist.html:
• Context Horowitz–Polchinski string stars qualitatively match black holes at the string scale; does this survive a twist $\nu$ of the thermal circle (imaginary angular velocity)?
  • Result
    • The lightest winding mode turns tachyonic at an exact $R_H(\nu)$: $R_H^2/\alpha'=4-2|\nu|+2\nu^2$ (bosonic), $2-2|\nu|$ (type II), heterotic the average of the two radii.
    • To order $\nu^2$ the Horowitz–Polchinski star, found numerically for $3\le d\le5$, gains a quadrupole that squashes it, and rotates rigidly, $J=\mathcal I\Omega$.
    • Extrapolated, its $J$ and eccentricity match Myers–Perry black holes and rotating free strings at leading order, up to $O(1)$ factors; its mass and entropy shifts have the opposite sign to the black hole's, which the paper argues is scheme dependent.
    • In AdS at real angular velocity $\Omega$, $R_H/l_s=\sqrt2-\frac{l_s}{2l_{ads}}(d-2+2\sqrt{1-\Omega^2})+O(\alpha'/l_{ads}^2)$.
  • Why it matters The rotating string star is proposed as the string-scale rotating Euclidean black hole, extending the correspondence's evidence to angular momentum.

student.html:
• Context Very hot, string-size black holes may turn into “string stars”, balls of strings held by their own gravity. Does this work when they spin?
  • Result
    • With an imaginary rotation $\nu$, strings wrapped around Euclidean time become unstable above an exact maximal (Hagedorn) temperature, for bosonic, type II and heterotic strings.
    • A slowly rotating string star is found numerically, spinning like a rigid body.
    • The star's rotation and flattening roughly match rotating black holes and free strings, linking the two.
    • In anti-de Sitter space, the curvature's leading correction to that temperature is computed.
  • Why it matters The rotating star could be what a rotating black hole becomes at string size.

brief.html:
A Euclidean black hole is described by Einstein gravity only while its inverse temperature $ eta$ is much larger than the string length $l_s$. Near the Hagedorn temperature, Horowitz and Polchinski proposed that it becomes a “string star”, a self-gravitating condensate of strings wound on the thermal circle, whose thermodynamics qualitatively matches the black hole's. The paper adds angular momentum. It fixes an imaginary angular velocity $ u$, with $ eta\Omega=2\pi i u$, the ensemble in which the rotating Euclidean black hole is real. Free strings then still have a Hagedorn temperature, now depending on $ u$; a rotating string star exists; and it qualitatively matches rotating black holes and rotating strings. So the string star remains a candidate description of the rotating black hole at string size.

Real angular velocity makes a flat-space ensemble diverge, as low-energy states can carry any angular momentum; imaginary $ u$ turns that weight into a phase. In Euclidean time the ensemble is flat space in which going once around the thermal circle rotates a plane by $2\pi u$, a Melvin space. The twist shifts the oscillator frequencies of strings wound on the circle, and the lightest wound string turns massless at $R_H^2/\alpha'=4-2| u|+2 u^2$ (bosonic) or $2-2| u|$ (type II), with $R_H= eta_H/2\pi$. For heterotic strings $R_H$ is the average of these two radii. Counting free-string states gives the same temperatures. At $ u=1$ the superstring trace becomes the supersymmetric index, where no instability is expected.

Reduced on the thermal circle, the twist becomes a Kaluza–Klein magnetic flux tube, and the winding mode gains a universal mass term growing as $ u^2 ho^2$ away from the rotation axis. Its lowest state is a Gaussian in the rotation plane, whose energy reproduces the $O( u)$ shift of the Hagedorn temperature in all three theories. At real angular velocity the same term is negative: the Euclidean face of the flat-space divergence. The effective theory holds only for $| u|\ll1$, where the Gaussian's width $\sqrt{\alpha'/| u|}$ exceeds the string length.

Close to $R_H( u)$ the winding mode is light, so the paper couples it to gravity and the dilaton and seeks a normalizable condensate. Treating $ u$ as a perturbation of the Horowitz–Polchinski solution, which exists for $3\le d\le5$ spatial dimensions, it solves the equations numerically to order $ u^2$. Rotation adds a quadrupole, making the star prolate at imaginary $ u$ and oblate once continued to real $\Omega$, like a slowly rotating Newtonian gas. The profile keeps the background's rotational symmetry and so has no intrinsic spin. Yet the star carries angular momentum of order $1/G_N$, $J=\mathcal I\Omega$, with $\mathcal I$ the Newtonian moment of inertia of its mass density. The Hagedorn relation $S= eta_HM$ still holds, and at fixed mass angular momentum lowers the entropy, since energy is spent on rotation.

Slowly rotating Myers–Perry black holes and the star, both extrapolated to $ eta\sim l_s$, are expanded in $l_s\Omega$. Their angular momentum and eccentricity, the only quantities shifted at leading order, agree up to order-one factors and in sign: both rotate along $\Omega$ and flatten. At subleading order mass and entropy rise with $\Omega$ for the star but fall for the black hole; moving the crossover point reverses this, so the paper calls such effects scheme dependent. On the other side, rotating free strings become self-gravitating at a breakdown mass, and there their angular velocity and eccentricity match the star's in $g_s$-scaling and sign.

In AdS the curvature confines the winding mode, so real angular velocities below the unitarity bound are stable, and the leading $l_s/l_{ads}$ shift of the Hagedorn temperature follows at real or imaginary rotation. For type II strings in pure NS-NS AdS$_3$, an exact $R_H( u)$ agrees with flat space for $k| u|>1$, where the paper reads a switch from long to short strings. Small AdS string stars and black holes look like flat-space ones, so the rotating correspondence is expected to carry over; the rotating AdS star is estimated, not solved.

Everything is perturbative in the rotation, so the regime $l_s\Omega\sim1$, where the crossover point itself moves, is out of reach. Only bosonic and type II stars are constructed; heterotic ones are believed similar. The matches extrapolate both saddles to where neither is reliable, so they are qualitative. Large angular momentum, up to the Regge bound, is left to speculation, such as a “stringy pancake” of near-extremal strings.

defs.html: A localised, self-gravitating condensate of strings wound around the Euclidean time circle, held together by the gravity it sources. It is a Euclidean saddle that exists just below the Hagedorn temperature, and a candidate for what a black hole becomes at string size.

The original, non-rotating string star (Horowitz and Polchinski, 1997): a normalizable condensate of the thermal winding mode bound by its own Newtonian potential, found near the Hagedorn temperature for $3\le d\le5$ spatial dimensions. The paper's rotating star is its perturbation in $\nu$.

A classical solution of the Euclidean action with the boundary conditions of the partition function; to leading order each contributes $e^{-I}$, with $I$ its on-shell action. Here three saddles share the twisted asymptotics: flat space with free strings, the rotating Euclidean black hole, and the rotating string star.

Euclidean time, periodic with length $\beta=1/T$ in a thermal partition function, so that a thermal system lives on $\mathbb R^d\times S^1_\beta$. Its radius is $R=\beta/2\pi$: smaller $R$ is hotter. Closed strings can wind around it, unlike particles.

The temperature above which the free-string partition function diverges, because the number of string states grows exponentially with energy. Equivalently, the temperature at which the string wound once around the thermal circle becomes massless. The paper finds how it depends on the imaginary angular velocity, $\beta_H(\nu)$.

The paper's new saddle: a string star whose asymptotic thermal circle is twisted by $\nu$, found to order $\nu^2$ around the Horowitz–Polchinski solution. Its profile has no intrinsic spin, yet it carries angular momentum $J=\mathcal I\Omega$, interpreted as a bound state of rotating strings.

at.quote: turns into a rotating string star

defs.html: The proposal that, as a Euclidean black hole heats up to the string scale, it turns continuously into a string star, which in turn becomes free strings at higher temperature or lower energy. The evidence is qualitative: both descriptions, extrapolated to where neither is reliable, roughly agree.

An angular velocity continued to imaginary values, $ eta\Omega=2\pi i
u$, so that the weight of a state with angular momentum $J$ is the phase $e^{2\pi i
u J}$ rather than an exponential. $
u=0$ is the ordinary thermal ensemble; for superstrings $
u=1$ gives $(-1)^F$, the supersymmetric index.

The boundary condition that realises the imaginary angular velocity geometrically: going once around the thermal circle also rotates the rotation plane by the angle $2\pi\nu$. The space stays locally flat; only the identification changes. The paper's results are expansions in this twist, $\nu\ll1$.

A closed string wrapped once around the thermal circle; its mass grows with the circle's radius. The lightest one, described by a complex scalar $\chi$, turns massless at the Hagedorn temperature and tachyonic above it. In this paper it is light, and its condensate is the string star.

The divergence of the free-string partition function above the Hagedorn temperature, seen in Euclidean language as the lightest winding mode turning tachyonic. The paper shows it survives at fixed imaginary angular velocity, except where the trace becomes the supersymmetric index.

The exponential growth of the number of string states with mass, $e^{\beta_HM}$, so that the entropy grows linearly, $S\approx\beta_HM$. It caps the temperature of a free-string gas at $1/\beta_H$; the paper finds the same growth at fixed angular momentum and at fixed $\nu$.

at.quote: Hagedorn growth of the partition function

defs.html: The Hagedorn temperature expressed as a radius of the thermal circle, $R_H=\beta_H/2\pi$, in string units $l_s=\sqrt{\alpha'}$. At $\nu=0$ it is $2$, $\sqrt2$ and $1+1/\sqrt2$ for bosonic, type II and heterotic strings. In section 3, $R_H$ denotes this $\nu=0$ value.

Treating a slowly rotating system as its non-rotating configuration turned bodily, so that $J=\mathcal I\Omega$ with $\mathcal I$ the moment of inertia of the unperturbed mass distribution. Centrifugal deformation changes energies only at order $\Omega^4$; the paper's star obeys this to order $\Omega^2$.

Angular momentum carried by the field profile itself, through an angular dependence such as $e^{im\phi}$. The rotating string star's winding profile has none: it keeps the background's rotation symmetry. Its angular momentum comes instead from the twisted background, like a rigid body's.

The maximal angular momentum of a string state of given mass, $J\le\frac12\alpha'M^2$ at large mass, reached by exciting only the oscillators of the rotation plane. States near it are nearly extremal and carry little entropy.

A measure of how flattened an object is: $e=\sqrt{1-L_\perp^2/L_{||}^2}$, with $L_{||}$ its size in the rotation plane and $L_\perp$ perpendicular to it. Zero for a round object; for slow rotation the paper finds $e$ linear in the angular momentum, for strings, string star and black hole alike.

Flat space with a circle along which one goes around while a plane rotates by a fixed angle. Reduced on that circle it becomes a magnetic flux tube (a fluxbrane) of the Kaluza–Klein gauge field, with a varying radius and dilaton. Here the circle is Euclidean time, which the paper notes is a new reading.

In an orbifold, the states of strings closed only up to the identification: here strings wound on the thermal circle, along which the rotation-plane coordinate returns rotated by $e^{2\pi i\nu}$. Their oscillators are shifted to frequencies $|n+\nu|$, which changes their zero-point energy and mass.

The projection onto states of definite worldsheet fermion number that makes superstring theory consistent and removes its tachyon. It depends on whether target-space fermions are periodic or antiperiodic around the thermal circle, which is why type II's lightest winding level depends on $\nu$.

The trace $\operatorname{Tr}(-1)^Fe^{-\beta H}$, in which bosons and fermions in supersymmetry multiplets cancel, so it does not depend on temperature. For superstrings it is reached at $\nu=1$, where $e^{2\pi iJ}=(-1)^F$; there the paper expects no Hagedorn instability.

Said of a saddle that is a local but not global minimum, or that decays at a rate invisible in perturbation theory. The rotating string star at real angular velocity is metastable: flat space at fixed real $\Omega$ is unstable, but the decay is non-perturbative in $\Omega$.

The range of temperatures, $\beta-\beta_H\sim l_s$, where a black hole has string-scale curvature and the string star is no longer close to the Hagedorn temperature, so neither description is reliable. The correspondence compares both saddles there by extrapolation.

Myers–Perry black holes are the rotating vacuum black holes of $D=d+1$ dimensions, generalising Kerr. The paper uses the one rotating in a single plane, slowly, so that its mass, entropy, angular momentum and shape can be expanded to order $\Omega^2$ at fixed temperature.

The mass at which a free string's own gravity can no longer be neglected: its gravitational energy reaches the spacing of string levels. For a random-walk string this is $l_sM\sim g_s^{4/(d-6)}$, where free strings are compared with the string star.

The regime of very large angular momentum, $J\sim M^2$ in string units, where rotating black holes in $D\ge6$ become very flat and highly rotating strings approach the Regge bound. Earlier work compared strings and black holes there; the paper's star does not reach it.

The paper's name for a speculative string star near the Regge bound: made of near-extremal strings with little entropy, flattened to eccentricity close to one, with thickness of order the string length. It is a guess, beyond the paper's control.

A highly rotating string configuration discussed in earlier work on rotating strings and black holes, into which the paper suggests a ‘stringy pancake’ string star near the Regge bound might turn. The paper uses both ‘bar’ and ‘rod’ for it.

Said of an AdS$_3$ background supported only by Neveu–Schwarz $B$-field flux, with no Ramond–Ramond flux. The worldsheet theory is then an exactly solvable $SL(2,\mathbb R)$ model, so the spectrum and Hagedorn temperature can be computed exactly. At $\Omega=0$ the winding mode there feels no confining potential.

In AdS$_3$ with NS-NS flux, strings that can grow to the boundary at little cost, in continuous representations of $SL(2,\mathbb R)$; short strings, in discrete representations, stay confined. The paper reads the jump in the second derivative of its exact $R_H^2(\nu)$ at $k|\nu|=1$ as the switch between them.

at.quote: from long strings to short strings

defs.html: The subgroup of the modular group $SL(2,\mathbb Z)$ generated by $S:\tau\to-1/\tau$ and $T^2:\tau\to\tau+2$: the transformations of the thermal torus that keep the fermions' boundary conditions, and so map string stars in AdS$_3$ to string stars.

questions.q: What do $\nu$, $R$, $m_0$ and $d$ mean, and which value of $\nu$ is which?
questions.a:
$
u$ is the imaginary angular velocity, $ eta\Omega=2\pi i
u$: $
u=0$ is the ordinary thermal ensemble, and “slow rotation” means $
u\ll1$. It is periodic, with period 1 for bosonic strings and 2 for superstrings, whose $
u=1$ is the supersymmetric index. $R= eta/2\pi$ is the thermal circle's radius and $R_H$ its Hagedorn value; $m_0^2=(R^2-R_H^2)/\alpha'^2$ measures the distance from it. $d$ counts spatial dimensions, $D=d+1$, and $l_s=\sqrt{\alpha'}$.

questions.q: Why fix an imaginary angular velocity rather than a real one?
questions.a: In flat space a real angular velocity makes the ensemble diverge: a state can carry huge angular momentum at little energy, and $e^{\beta\Omega J}$ then wins. An imaginary one turns that weight into a phase, so Hagedorn growth can dominate again. It is also the ensemble in which the rotating Euclidean black hole is a real geometry. Results computed perturbatively in $\nu$ are then continued back to small real $\Omega$.

questions.q: Why does a small rotation raise the Hagedorn temperature?
questions.a: In state counting, the phases $e^{2\pi i\nu J}$ partly cancel the sum over states and suppress its divergence. In the Euclidean picture, the twist confines the winding mode near the rotation axis, like a harmonic potential, which raises its mass by $2|\nu|/\alpha'$. A smaller thermal circle, a higher temperature, is then needed before it turns massless.

questions.q: Why does the type II Hagedorn temperature become infinite at $\nu=1$?
questions.a: At $\nu=1$ the rotation weight is $(-1)^F$, so target-space fermions are periodic and the trace is the supersymmetric index. Bosons and fermions cancel, the result cannot depend on temperature, and there is no Hagedorn instability. In the formula, the wound string becomes massless only at $R=0$; T-dually it is a graviton momentum mode, massless in the decompactified limit. Heterotic strings likewise have no instability there.

questions.q: Does the target-space effective theory reproduce the exact $R_H(\nu)$?
questions.a:
No, only its first order in $
u$. At leading order in $\alpha'$ the twist enters only through the metric, which reproduces the $O(
u)$ mass shift exactly; higher orders need couplings such as $\alpha'F^2|\chi|^2$ to the Kaluza–Klein field strength, which are not derived. The paper expects finitely many to give the exact answer, but stresses that the theory is invalid for generic $
u$.

questions.q: How can a star whose profile has no intrinsic spin carry angular momentum?
questions.a: The profile keeps the background's rotation symmetry, so it has no angular dependence of its own. The angular momentum comes from the twisted boundary condition: the action depends on $\nu$ through a $\rho^2|\chi|^2$ term, and differentiating it gives $J=\mathcal I\Omega$. The moment of inertia is exactly the Newtonian one of the star's mass density, so it rotates like a rigid body.

questions.q: Why is the star prolate at imaginary $\nu$ but oblate at real $\Omega$?
questions.a: A slowly rotating self-gravitating gas is pushed outwards by centrifugal force: it thins at the centre and bulges at the equator, both effects of order $\Omega^2$. With $\Omega$ imaginary, $\Omega^2$ is negative, so the signs flip: the computed star is denser at the centre and the poles and thinner at the equator. Continued to real $\Omega$ it becomes oblate, as intuition expects.

questions.q: Why is the star found only for $3\le d\le5$, and what about $d=2$?
questions.a: The perturbation starts from the Horowitz–Polchinski solution, which is normalizable only for $3\le d\le5$; for $d\ge6$ no self-consistent solution exists, as it always tends to shrink. For $d=2$ the rotating equations resemble those of the AdS$_3$ string star, so a solution exists, but it has no non-rotating limit and lies outside the slow-rotation expansion.

questions.q: Why is there no heterotic rotating string star?
questions.a: The heterotic winding mode also carries half a unit of momentum around the thermal circle, so it couples to the Kaluza–Klein vector, which the twist turns on. That makes its equations more complicated, and the paper builds only the bosonic and type II stars. It believes the difference is not essential and that a heterotic star exists with similar properties, but does not construct it.

questions.q: Doesn't the opposite sign of the subleading mass and entropy shifts contradict the correspondence?
questions.a: Not necessarily. Where the two saddles are compared is fixed only up to order-one factors, and the choice can itself depend on $\Omega$. Defining the crossover as the point where the horizon radius equals $l_s$ shifts the black hole's temperature at order $\alpha'\Omega^2$, after which its mass and entropy also rise with $\Omega$. So subleading effects are scheme dependent; the free-string side behaves similarly.

questions.q: What does the paper not show?
questions.a: That the star and the black hole are continuously connected: the comparisons extrapolate both to where neither is reliable. Everything is to order $\Omega^2$, so large rotation, $l_s\Omega\sim1$ or the Regge bound, is speculation. No heterotic star is built, the rotating AdS star is only estimated, and the star's one-loop determinant is not computed. An earlier worldsheet argument against a smooth transition in type II is believed to carry over.

questions.q: How does this differ from earlier work on rotating strings and spinning condensates?
questions.a: Earlier work by Čeplak, Emparan, Puhm and Tomašević compared rotating black holes directly with free strings, including near extremality, varying the coupling at fixed entropy. Here the comparison is with the string star, at small rotation and fixed coupling. Santos and Zigdon sought a spinning heterotic condensate with no asymptotic twist, so it needed intrinsic spin; here the twist is asymptotic and the profile has none.

questions.q: Why can AdS work with a real angular velocity when flat space cannot?
questions.a: In AdS the winding mode's mass grows away from the centre because of the curvature, and this outweighs the centrifugal term as long as $\Omega<1$ in AdS units. That bound is the CFT's unitarity bound $E\ge J$. So the ensemble is stable, the Hagedorn temperature can be computed directly at real $\Omega$, and near it the rotating string star should exist without continuing to imaginary angular velocity.
